title: State Machines
description: Registers, synchronous counters and finite state machines: state tables, Moore and Mealy machines and clock timing.

study.title: Registers and shift registers
study.body: A **register** is a row of $n$ D flip-flops with a common clock: it stores a word of $n$ bits and loads all bits in parallel at the active edge. In a **shift register** each flip-flop takes its D input from its neighbour, so every clock edge moves the word one place. Shifting an unsigned number left (a 0 enters at the LSB) multiplies it by 2 and loses the MSB; shifting right divides by 2 and drops the LSB. Shift registers convert serial data to parallel and back (UART, SPI).

study.title: Synchronous counters
study.body: In a **synchronous** counter all flip-flops share the clock, so all bits change together after one clock-to-Q delay (no ripple). Built from T flip-flops, bit $i$ toggles at an active edge when all lower bits are 1. An $n$-bit binary counter has $2^n$ states, and $Q_i$ is a square wave at $f_{clk}/2^{i+1}$. A mod-$M$ counter needs $n = \lceil \log_2 M \rceil$ flip-flops. The timing diagram shows a 3-bit up counter (rising-edge triggered).

study.title: Finite state machines
study.body: A synchronous **finite state machine** (FSM) is a state register (flip-flops) plus combinational **next-state logic** and **output logic**. At every active clock edge the register loads the next state $S^+ = f(S, x)$. A **state diagram** draws states as circles and transitions as arrows labelled with the input; a **state table** lists $S^+$ (and the output) for every present state and input. With $N_S$ states, binary encoding needs $\lceil \log_2 N_S \rceil$ flip-flops, one-hot encoding needs $N_S$.

study.title: Moore vs Mealy
study.body: In a **Moore** machine the output depends only on the present state: it is written inside the state circle ($S_2/1$) and changes only just after clock edges. In a **Mealy** machine the output depends on the state **and** the present input: it is written on the arrows ($x/z$, e.g. $1/1$) and can change as soon as the input changes, even between edges. A Mealy machine usually needs fewer states and responds one clock earlier; a Moore machine gives glitch-free, synchronous outputs.

study.title: Designing a sequence detector
study.body: Example: a Mealy machine that outputs $z$ = 1 when the last three inputs were 101 (overlap allowed). $S_0$: nothing useful seen, $S_1$: last input 1, $S_2$: last inputs 10. From $S_2$ an input 1 completes 101, gives $z = 1$ and goes to $S_1$, because that final 1 can start the next 101. Then: assign binary codes to the states, write next-state and output equations (K-maps) and use D flip-flops with $D = S^+$. The table entries are $S^+/z$.

study.title: Maximum clock frequency
study.body: Between two active edges a new state must leave the flip-flop (clock-to-Q delay $t_{cq}$), pass through the slowest combinational path ($t_{pd,max}$) and be stable a setup time $t_{su}$ before the next edge. So the clock period must be at least the sum. Example: $t_{cq}$ = 1 ns, $t_{pd}$ = 4 ns, $t_{su}$ = 0.5 ns give $T_{clk} \ge$ 5.5 ns, $f_{max}$ = 182 MHz. (Data must also stay stable for the hold time $t_h$ after the edge.)
study.formula: \begin{array}{c} T_{clk} \ge t_{cq} + t_{pd,max} + t_{su} \\[4pt] f_{max} = \dfrac{1}{t_{cq} + t_{pd,max} + t_{su}} \end{array}

steps.title: Synchronous counters
steps.body: In a ripple counter each flip-flop is clocked by the previous one, so the delays add up. In a **synchronous** counter every flip-flop gets the same clock and all bits change together. The logic in front of each flip-flop decides **whether** it toggles: with T flip-flops, bit $Q_i$ toggles when all lower bits are 1 (just like a carry in binary addition).
steps.formula: T_0 = 1,\quad T_1 = Q_0,\quad T_2 = Q_0Q_1,\quad T_3 = Q_0Q_1Q_2

steps.prompt: A 4-bit synchronous up counter is built from T flip-flops that share one clock. When does $Q_3$ toggle?
options: At an active clock edge when $Q_0 = Q_1 = Q_2 = 1$
At an active clock edge when $Q_2 = 1$
steps.explanation: $T_3 = Q_0Q_1Q_2$: the MSB toggles only on the edge that takes the count from $x111$ to the next value (e.g. $0111 \to 1000$), just like a carry ripples into the next column. 'Every edge' describes $Q_0$, and 'when $Q_2$ falls' is how a **ripple** counter is clocked, not a synchronous one.

steps.prompt: The timing diagram shows a 3-bit synchronous counter (rising-edge triggered). What count $Q_2Q_1Q_0$ does it hold at $t_1$? Give it as a decimal number.
steps.explanation: Read the three outputs on the line $t_1$: $Q_2$ = {{mod(floor(mod(s0+k+1,8)/4),2)}}, $Q_1$ = {{mod(floor(mod(s0+k+1,8)/2),2)}}, $Q_0$ = {{mod(floor(mod(s0+k+1,8)/1),2)}}. With $Q_2$ as the MSB: $4\cdot${{mod(floor(mod(s0+k+1,8)/4),2)}} + $2\cdot${{mod(floor(mod(s0+k+1,8)/2),2)}} + {{mod(floor(mod(s0+k+1,8)/1),2)}} = **{{mod(s0+k+1,8)}}**. The outputs change only just after the rising clock edges, and the count goes up by one each time (wrapping from 7 to 0).

steps.prompt: A controller is designed as a state machine with {{N}} states.

ask.prompt: How many flip-flops does it need at least with **binary** state encoding?
ask.explanation: $n$ flip-flops give $2^n$ codes, so we need $2^n \ge$ {{N}}: $2^{ {{ceil(ln(N)/ln(2))-1}} }$ = {{2^(ceil(ln(N)/ln(2))-1)}} is too few, $2^{ {{ceil(ln(N)/ln(2))}} }$ = {{2^ceil(ln(N)/ln(2))}} is enough, so $n = \lceil \log_2 {{N}} \rceil$ = **{{ceil(ln(N)/ln(2))}}**.

ask.prompt: How many flip-flops does it need with **one-hot** encoding (one flip-flop per state)?
ask.explanation: One-hot encoding uses one flip-flop per state, exactly one of which is 1, so **{{N}}** flip-flops. That is more than the {{ceil(ln(N)/ln(2))}} needed with binary encoding, but the next-state logic becomes very simple and fast.

steps.title: State tables
steps.body: A state machine is described by a **state table**: for every present state $S$ (row) and input $x$ (column) it gives the next state $S^+$ that is loaded at the next active clock edge; the last column is the Moore output $z$. This Moore machine sets $z$ = 1 after it has sampled two 1s in a row: $S_0$ = 'last input 0', $S_1$ = 'one 1', $S_2$ = 'two or more 1s'.
steps.formula: \begin{array}{c|cc|c} S & x=0 & x=1 & z \\ \hline S_0 & S_0 & S_1 & 0 \\ S_1 & S_0 & S_2 & 0 \\ S_2 & S_0 & S_2 & 1 \end{array}

steps.prompt:
Using the table, the machine is in state $S_{{{s}}}$ and $x$ = {{x}} at the next rising clock edge. What is the state, and the output $z$, after the edge?
$$\begin{array}{c|cc|c} S & x=0 & x=1 & z \\ \hline S_0 & S_0 & S_1 & 0 \\ S_1 & S_0 & S_2 & 0 \\ S_2 & S_0 & S_2 & 1 \end{array}$$
steps.explanation: Look up row $S_{{{s}}}$, column $x$ = {{x}}: $S^+ = S_{ {{x*(1+min(1,s))}} }$. In a Moore machine the output belongs to the state, so $z$ is read from the new state's row: $z$ = {{step(x*(1+min(1,s))-1.5)}}.

steps.prompt: Match each part of a synchronous state machine to its job.
pairs: Flip-flops that hold the present state
Decides when the state is updated
steps.explanation: The state register stores $S$. Combinational next-state logic computes $S^+ = f(S, x)$, and the register loads it at the active clock edge. Output logic computes $z = g(S)$ (Moore) or $z = g(S, x)$ (Mealy).

steps.title: Moore and Mealy machines
steps.body:
**Moore:** the output depends only on the state. It is written in the state circle ($S_2/1$) and can change only just after a clock edge.
**Mealy:** the output depends on the state and the present input. It is written on the arrows ($x/z$), so it can react to an input change straight away, without waiting for the next edge. Mealy machines often need fewer states.

steps.prompt: The output of a Mealy machine can change between two clock edges.
steps.explanation: True. A Mealy output $z = g(S, x)$ depends directly on the input, so when $x$ changes in the middle of a clock period, $z$ can change too. A Moore output $z = g(S)$ only changes when the state changes, i.e. just after an active edge.

steps.prompt: In a state diagram the arrows are labelled like $1/0$ and $0/1$, and the circles only carry state names. What kind of machine is it?
options: It is not a state machine, but a counter
steps.explanation: An arrow label $x/z$ means 'with input $x$, output $z$ while taking this transition'. The output depends on the state **and** the input, which is a Mealy machine. A Moore machine writes the output inside the state circle.

steps.prompt: In a synchronous circuit the flip-flops have $t_{cq}$ = {{tcq|s}} and $t_{su}$ = {{tsu|s}}. The slowest combinational path between two flip-flops has a delay of {{tpd|s}}. What is the maximum clock frequency?

This Mealy machine detects the input sequence 101. Entries are $S^+/z$. It is in state $S_{{{s}}}$ and the input is $x$ = {{x}}. What are the next state and the output $z$?
$$\begin{array}{c|cc} S & x=0 & x=1 \\ \hline S_0 & S_0/0 & S_1/0 \\ S_1 & S_2/0 & S_1/0 \\ S_2 & S_0/0 & S_1/1 \end{array}$$
steps.explanation: Read row $S_{{{s}}}$, column $x$ = {{x}}. In a Mealy machine the output is part of the transition ($S^+/z$), so it depends on both the state and the present input. Only the transition $S_2 \xrightarrow{1} S_1$ completes 101 and gives $z$ = 1.

steps.prompt: The Mealy 101 detector (overlap allowed) starts in $S_0$ and receives the input sequence {{b0}} {{b1}} {{b2}} {{b3}} {{b4}} {{b5}} {{b6}} {{b7}} (first bit first). How many times does it output $z$ = 1?
steps.explanation: Every time the last three inputs read 101, $z$ = 1. Because the machine goes to $S_1$ after a detection, overlapping patterns count (10101 contains two). Slide a 3-bit window along the input: {{b0}}{{b1}}{{b2}}, {{b1}}{{b2}}{{b3}}, {{b2}}{{b3}}{{b4}}, {{b3}}{{b4}}{{b5}}, {{b4}}{{b5}}{{b6}}, {{b5}}{{b6}}{{b7}}. The number of windows equal to 101 is **{{b0*(1-b1)*b2 + b1*(1-b2)*b3 + b2*(1-b3)*b4 + b3*(1-b4)*b5 + b4*(1-b5)*b6 + b5*(1-b6)*b7}}**.

steps.prompt: A design must run at {{f|Hz}}. Its flip-flops have $t_{cq}$ = {{tcq|s}} and $t_{su}$ = {{tsu|s}}. What is the largest allowed delay of the combinational logic between two flip-flops?
steps.explanation:
$T_{clk} = 1/f$ = {{1/f|s}}. The logic gets what is left after the flip-flop overheads:
$t_{pd,max} = T_{clk} - t_{cq} - t_{su}$ = {{1/f|s}} − {{tcq|s}} − {{tsu|s}} = **{{1/f-tcq-tsu|s}}**.

steps.prompt: An 8-bit shift register holds the unsigned number {{N}}.

ask.prompt: It is shifted **left** {{k}} times, with a 0 entering at the LSB each time. What number (decimal) does it hold now?
ask.explanation: Each left shift doubles the number, and bits shifted out of the top are lost (only 8 bits fit): {{N}} × $2^{ {{k}} }$ = {{N*2^k||5}}, modulo 256: **{{mod(N*2^k,256)}}**.

ask.prompt: It is shifted **right** {{k}} times, with a 0 entering at the MSB each time. What number (decimal) does it hold now?
ask.explanation: Each right shift halves the number and drops the LSB: $\lfloor {{N}} / 2^{ {{k}} } \rfloor$ = $\lfloor$ {{N/2^k||6}} $\rfloor$ = **{{floor(N/2^k)}}**.

steps.prompt: A synchronous mod-{{M}} counter (states 0 to {{M-1}}) is clocked at {{f|Hz}}. It produces one terminal-count pulse each time it passes from {{M-1}} back to 0. What is the frequency of these pulses?
steps.explanation: The counter needs {{M}} clock periods for a full cycle, so the terminal-count output divides the clock by {{M}}: $f_{TC} = f_{clk}/M$ = {{f|Hz}}/{{M}} = **{{f/M|Hz}}**. (This is how clock dividers and timers are made.)

steps.prompt: Put the steps of designing a synchronous state machine in order.
items: Draw the state diagram from the specification
Assign a binary code to each state
Derive the next-state and output equations (K-maps)
Draw the circuit with D flip-flops and gates
steps.explanation: First capture the behaviour (diagram, then table). Only then choose state codes, because the equations depend on them. Minimise the next-state and output logic with K-maps, and finally connect the gates to D flip-flops ($D = S^+$).

steps.prompt: Flip-flops with $t_{cq}$ = {{tcq|s}} and $t_{su}$ = {{tsu|s}} are connected through logic with a worst-case delay of {{tpd|s}}. The circuit works correctly at a clock frequency of {{f|Hz}}.
steps.explanation: The required period is $t_{cq} + t_{pd} + t_{su}$ = {{tcq+tpd+tsu|s}} ($f_{max}$ = {{1/(tcq+tpd+tsu)|Hz}}). The clock period is $1/f$ = {{1/f|s}}, which leaves a slack of {{(1/f-tcq-tpd-tsu)*1e9}} ns. Positive slack: it works; negative slack: setup is violated.

steps.prompt: A **Moore** machine must output $z$ = 1 for one clock period after it has received the sequence 101 (overlap allowed). What is the minimum number of states?
steps.explanation: The Mealy version needs 3 states ($S_0$, seen 1, seen 10) because the output sits on the transition. A Moore output belongs to a state, so a 4th state 'just seen 101' with $z$ = 1 is needed. From it, input 0 leads to 'seen 10' and input 1 to 'seen 1' (overlap).

steps.prompt: In the Mealy 101 detector, the transition from $S_2$ ('seen 10') with input 1 outputs $z$ = 1 and goes to $S_1$ ('seen 1') rather than back to $S_0$. Why?
options: The final 1 of 101 can also be the first 1 of the next 101
steps.explanation: With overlap allowed, 10101 must give two detections. After 101 the most recent input is a 1, which is exactly the situation 'seen 1' = $S_1$. Going to $S_0$ would throw that 1 away and miss the second 101.

steps.prompt: The Moore machine from the state table ($S_0 \to S_1 \to S_2$ on 1s, back to $S_0$ on a 0) outputs $z$ = 1 in $S_2$, i.e. when the last **two** samples of $x$ were 1. It samples $x$ at the rising edges of CLK and starts in $S_0$. Which graph shows $z$?
steps.explanation: Sample $x$ at each rising edge ($t$ = 1, 3, 5, …). $z$ becomes 1 just after the **second** edge in a row at which $x$ = 1, and stays 1 until an edge samples a 0. A Moore output only changes at clock edges, so the graph with steps between the edges belongs to a Mealy machine. The other graphs are one clock late, or react to a single 1.

steps.prompt: An {{n}}-bit synchronous counter uses T flip-flops with $T_i = T_{i-1} Q_{i-1}$, built as a chain of 2-input AND gates ($T_2 = Q_0Q_1$ needs one gate, $T_3 = T_2 Q_2$ a second gate, …). Each AND gate has a delay of {{tand|s}}; the flip-flops have $t_{cq}$ = {{tcq|s}} and $t_{su}$ = {{tsu|s}}. What is the maximum clock frequency?

A machine with state bits $Q_1Q_0$, input $x$ and D flip-flops has the next-state equations below. What does it do?
$$D_0 = Q_0 \oplus x, \qquad D_1 = Q_1 \oplus (Q_0\,x)$$
options: It counts up (mod 4) on every edge where $x$ = 1, and holds when $x$ = 0
It sets $Q_1Q_0$ = 11 after two 1s and resets on a 0
steps.explanation: $D_0 = Q_0 \oplus x$: $Q_0$ toggles when $x$ = 1. $D_1 = Q_1 \oplus Q_0x$: $Q_1$ toggles when $x$ = 1 **and** $Q_0$ = 1. That is exactly the T-flip-flop rule of a synchronous up counter ($T_0 = x$, $T_1 = xQ_0$), so $x$ acts as a count enable.

steps.prompt: The machine with $D_0 = Q_0 \oplus x$ and $D_1 = Q_1 \oplus (Q_0 x)$ starts in state $Q_1Q_0$ = {{floor(s0/2)}}{{mod(s0,2)}}. At five successive rising edges $x$ is {{b0}}, {{b1}}, {{b2}}, {{b3}}, {{b4}}. What is the state $Q_1Q_0$ afterwards, as a decimal number?
steps.explanation: The machine is a mod-4 up counter with enable $x$: it starts at {{s0}} and counts every edge with $x$ = 1. There are {{b0+b1+b2+b3+b4}} such edges, so the state is ({{s0}} + {{b0+b1+b2+b3+b4}}) mod 4 = **{{mod(s0+b0+b1+b2+b3+b4,4)}}**, i.e. $Q_1Q_0$ = {{floor(mod(s0+b0+b1+b2+b3+b4,4)/2)}}{{mod(s0+b0+b1+b2+b3+b4,2)}}.

steps.prompt: The Moore '11' machine ($z$ = 1 in $S_2$ when the last two samples were 1) starts in $S_0$ and samples {{b0}} {{b1}} {{b2}} {{b3}} {{b4}} {{b5}} {{b6}} {{b7}} at eight successive rising edges. For how many of the eight clock periods that follow these edges is $z$ = 1?
steps.explanation: After an edge the machine is in $S_2$ when that sample **and** the one before were both 1. Count the adjacent pairs 11 in the sequence (overlapping: 111 gives two): pairs {{b0}}{{b1}}, {{b1}}{{b2}}, {{b2}}{{b3}}, {{b3}}{{b4}}, {{b4}}{{b5}}, {{b5}}{{b6}}, {{b6}}{{b7}} → **{{b0*b1 + b1*b2 + b2*b3 + b3*b4 + b4*b5 + b5*b6 + b6*b7}}** periods with $z$ = 1.
